To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rate of protein fiber formation is accelerated by inert cosolutes that occupy a high fraction of the volume of the reaction vessel, that the extent of acceleration is sensitive to several parameters, and that the effect of crowding is to accelerate the rate of polymerization without affecting the rate of redistribution.

the rate of protein fiber formation in a crowded solution can be increased by as much as two orders of magnitude relative to that in a dilute solution, but that the rate of fiber length redistribution in a crowded solution is essentially the same as that in a dilution solution.

volume-excluding macromoecules can accelerate the rate at which protein fiber forms by several orders of magnitude but have little effect on the rate of redistribution, and that the acceleration is most pronounced for proteins that form fibers through the association of a large number of monomers to form a large nucleus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the kinetics of protein fiber formation in the presence of inert macromolecules that occupy a large fraction of the total available volume.
the effects of inert macromolecules on the rates of protein polymerization and the rates of protein fiber growth.
understanding how protein fiber formation is affected by macromolecular crowding and with developing a kinetic model that is consistent with the experimental observations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

macromolecular crowding can accelerate protein polymerization by several orders of magnitude, and that the extent of the acceleration depends upon the stoichiometry, shape, size, and reversibility of the nucleus, as well as upon the shape, size, volume fraction, and degree of volume occupancy of the crowding agent.

macromolecular crowding is a general phenomenon which has profound effects upon the rates of polymerization processes, but that the effects depend upon many factors, including the nature of the macromolecule and the nature of the inert cosolute.
crowding accelerates the rate of polymer formation but has no effect on polymer redistribution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the rate of polymer formation can be accelerated by as much as 10(5)-fold by the presence of inert volume-excluded macromolecules and that the rate of redistribution is unaffected by the presence of these cosolutes.
volume exclusion can be an important factor in the kinetics of nucleated polymerization, but only if the nucleus is small relative to the size of the fiber-forming monomer.
volume occupancy by inert cosolutes can have a profound effect on the kinetics of nucleated polymer formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
volume-excluding cosolutes have a strong influence on the kinetics of fiber formation, but not on the kinetics of redistribution of fiber lengths.
the rate of nucleated polymerization is highly sensitive to the extent of volume occupancy by macromolecular cosolute.
the rate of fiber polymerization is sensitive to the degree of volume occupancy and that the extent of acceleration depends upon the stoichiometry and size of the nucleus.
